title: Win More Often by Not Trying To
author: Admired Leadership
summary: A short argument for process over outcome, built on the paradox in its title. The author's claim is that wanting something badly puts a person at odds with getting it, because fixating on victory or on being seen as great diverts attention from the execution that actually produces victory. The reasoning rests on a control distinction: outcomes, accolades and the win itself are not ours to command, while the steps leading to them are. Long-term winners and the acknowledged greats of any field are offered as evidence — they are described as winning not by wanting to but by earning the right to win through successive acts of excellence, with Bill Walsh's dictum that the score will take care of itself supplied as the compressed version. A careful qualification keeps the piece from collapsing into passivity: the desire to win is called essential, and it is only the focus on winning that interferes. The closing formulation inverts the usual motivational advice — knowing how to perform at your best matters more than wanting to be the best.
points: The argument turns on a control distinction rather than on modesty: outcomes and accolades cannot be commanded, only the successive steps that produce them.
The author explicitly preserves ambition while rejecting its object — desire to win is essential, focus on winning is the distraction.
Bill Walsh's 'the score will take care of itself' is used as the compressed statement of the whole case, tying the claim to a practitioner rather than a theory.
Performers studied across fields are said to earn the right to win through each successive action, which reframes greatness as accumulated execution rather than intent.
Self-mastery is equated with mastery of the process, making the personal discipline and the competitive result the same project.
quotes: What is hard for most people to accept is that obsessing on success is a surefire way not to attain it.
We don’t control the outcomes, accolades, or the victory. We only control the steps it takes to get there.
They win and become great by focusing on the steps it takes to perform each and every moment with excellence.
The desire to win is essential, but the focus on winning gets in the way.
Any time the victory or triumph becomes the center of our attention, we take our eyes off of execution.
As it turns out, knowing how to perform at your best is more important than your desire to be the best.
